Common questions

What's the difference between gross and net revenue retention?

Gross revenue retention (GRR) answers one question only: of the MRR you started the month with, how much did you keep, counting only contraction and churn against it? It never counts new, expansion, or reactivation MRR, and it is capped at 100% because you cannot retain more of a base than you started with. Net revenue retention (NRR) adds expansion and reactivation back in and has no cap. On the default example, GRR is 90% (real churn and contraction) while NRR is 106% (expansion and reactivation more than covered it) -- both numbers are correct, and they answer different questions.

Why can net revenue retention be over 100%?

Because expansion and reactivation MRR are added to the base before comparing it to what you started with. When existing customers upgrade or come back for more than the contraction and churn removed, the surviving base is worth more than it was a month ago -- this is what SaaS operators mean by “negative churn.” It is a real, common, and desirable outcome. It does not mean nothing was lost; check gross revenue retention for that.

Does new MRR count toward NRR or GRR?

No. Both retention metrics measure what happened to the base of customers you already had at the start of the period. New MRR from brand-new customers is a separate line in the waterfall (and in ending MRR and the quick ratio), but it is never part of either retention percentage -- a period with excellent retention and zero new customers still reports the same GRR and NRR as one with the same retention and a wave of new signups.

What does the quick ratio tell me that retention doesn't?

Retention is about the existing base only. The quick ratio -- growth MRR (new plus expansion plus reactivation) divided by loss MRR (contraction plus churn) -- adds new customers back into the picture and asks a blunter question: for every dollar you lost, how many did you win? A ratio above 4 is generally considered strong, 1 means you are running in place, and below 1 means you are shrinking even after counting new business.

Is my subscription data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. The six numbers you type in are never sent anywhere, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your MRR figures.

MRR Waterfall Calculator vs. tracking MRR in a spreadsheet

Most SaaS operators already track MRR in a spreadsheet: a column for starting MRR, one each for new, expansion, contraction, and churn, and a formula or two for the totals. Every one of those formulas is ordinary arithmetic. Where a spreadsheet formula goes wrong is not the arithmetic — it's keeping new, expansion, and reactivation MRR out of gross revenue retention specifically, which is the one rule that makes gross retention mean something different from net retention.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every formula this calculator runs — the waterfall total, gross and net revenue retention, and the quick ratio. Building it correctly means writing two separate retention formulas (one excluding growth, one including it), remembering to cap only the gross one at 100%, and never letting a copy-and-edit of one formula quietly turn into the other.

This calculator keeps the six inputs, the full waterfall, and both retention percentages on one screen, with the exclusion rule built into the tool itself rather than into a formula that can drift.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's my gross revenue retention this period, excluding growth?This calculator's readout — the exclusion is enforced in code, not a formula.
What's my net revenue retention, including expansion and winbacks?The same readout, computed independently from the same six inputs.
How do I compare several periods or cohorts side by side?A spreadsheet you build yourself — this tool answers one period at a time.
Am I over- or under-charging existing customers on price?The subscription price impact calculator.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

Worked example

Starting MRR of $10,000, with $1,200 in new MRR, $1,500 in expansion, $100 reactivated, $400 in contraction, and $600 churned this period:

LineAmount
Starting MRR$10,000.00
+ New / Expansion / Reactivation+$2,800.00
- Contraction / Churn-$1,000.00
= Ending MRR$11,800.00
Gross revenue retention90.0%
Net revenue retention106.0%

A single retention formula built by copying one cell and swapping the numerator would report the same 106% for both rows, hiding the fact that this period actually lost 10% of its starting base to real churn and contraction — the exact distinction a board update or investor update needs, and the one a rebuilt spreadsheet formula most often collapses into one number.

This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic method of tracking these numbers in a spreadsheet, not a competing calculator or platform.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet compute the same waterfall?

Yes. Starting MRR plus new, expansion, and reactivation, minus contraction and churn, is ordinary addition and subtraction. The retention percentages and the quick ratio are ordinary division. Every formula this calculator runs can be written in a spreadsheet cell.

What does a spreadsheet not enforce that this calculator does?

That new, expansion, and reactivation MRR never enter the gross revenue retention formula. A spreadsheet has no rule against summing the wrong column into the wrong cell, and the easiest mistake to make by hand is building one retention formula, copying it, and only changing the numerator -- which silently turns gross retention into a second copy of net retention. This calculator computes both from the same six inputs with the exclusion built into the code, not into a formula a future edit can quietly break.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when you need more than one period side by side, a cohort-level breakdown by signup month, or a chart of the trend over time. This calculator answers one period at a time and does not store or chart history. A spreadsheet you build yourself can track as many periods and cohorts as you want.

Is my MRR data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. The six numbers you type in are never sent anywhere, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your MRR figures.
